source.title: Hardware Co-Design Scaling Laws via Roofline Modelling for On-Device LLMs
source.authors: Luo-Yang Sun; Jiwen Jiang; Yi-Feng Ding; Feng-Fa Li; Yan-Ke Song; Hai-Feng Zhang; Jian Ying; Lei Ren; Kun Zhan; Wei Chen; Yan Xie; Cheng Deng

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses empirical scaling-law fitting as a tool for a different goal: predicting architecture-level loss and combining it with hardware latency models for on-device architecture selection. It does not test the specified parameter/token/compute laws or their compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper fits loss against architecture variables with training tokens and optimization held fixed. Its held-out configurations are not runs orders of magnitude larger, and it does not report a loss-minimising parameter/token split as compute varies. It describes architecture-dependent loss results, but does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count as V4 requires. The WikiText-2 perplexity comparison and latency/Pareto results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper fits its own loss model over architecture variables (depth, width, MoE sparsity, FFN ratio, KV dimension) at a fixed 10B-token budget. It uses that fit as a surrogate for hardware-aware Pareto search. It never varies tokens or compute. It does not fit loss against parameter count, extrapolate to much larger runs, or derive a compute-optimal split. It does not compare shapes at matched parameter count: depth 4–32 and width 768–3072 change size as well as shape. Its reported results are fit R², fitted exponents, Pareto frontiers and a WikiText-2 comparison, all serving its own method.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors also claim the fitted law enables extrapolation of optimal designs across deployment regimes. They caveat that it may not hold at different training budgets or data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits a separable polynomial-style loss model over architecture variables at a fixed 10B-token budget, then combines it with roofline latency modeling; it does not reproduce the original parameter/data/compute scaling-law procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that their fitted loss law is based on 170 architectures trained for 10B tokens and caution that prediction accuracy may decline with substantially different training budgets or data distributions. Training-count details differ within the text: the fitting description gives 120 training and 17 validation configurations, while the Figure 4 caption gives 138 training and 32 held-out configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: A separable power-law-style model in architecture variables fits validation loss of 170 dense and MoE models at 10B tokens (train R² 0.975, held-out R² 0.952).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed token budget, loss across dense and MoE architectures is predictable from a separable function of depth, width, sparsity, FFN ratio and KV dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted exponents show strong depth dependence (1.63), a width–sparsity coupling (β1=−0.33), a weak FFN-ratio effect (0.17) and a minimal KV-cache effect (0.05).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In fixed-budget training of small dense and MoE models, the loss contributions of architecture dimensions differ greatly in size.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and checkpoints will be made publicly available
record.problems: The text gives inconsistent fitting and validation configuration counts (120/17 in the methods text versus 138/32 in the Figure 4 caption). The paper notes that prediction may be less accurate at substantially different training budgets or data distributions. It reports no uncertainty intervals for the fitted coefficients or R² values.
record.rows_left_out: The WikiText-2 perplexity comparison (50.88 vs. 63.14) and latency/Pareto results are omitted because they do not test any listed version's scaling or predictability claim.

untested.parts: Tokens are fixed at 10B and loss is not fitted against parameter count or compute.
There is no extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute budget is not varied and no parameter/token split is reported.
No comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
Text-only LM pretraining in a single regime.
The only downstream result is one WikiText-2 perplexity comparison against Qwen2.5-0.5B at matched latency. There is no scale trend.
Fitting choices and setups are not compared.

record.verdict_notes: There are internal inconsistencies. The fit/held-out counts are 120/17 in the text versus 138/32 in the Figure 4 caption. Validation loss is averaged over the final 10 steps in Section 4.1.1 but over the final 1,000 steps in Appendix B. No uncertainty is given for the coefficients. The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only to contrast its deployment-focused aim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper holds the training-token budget at 10B and does not test held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameter count, tokens, or training compute.
Held-out configurations are not runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
It does not vary training compute budgets to find optimal parameter and token allocations or their growth rates.
It varies architecture variables and fits their relation to loss, but does not report controlled comparisons at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text-model architecture search under one fixed pretraining regime, not other modalities or the listed training regimes.
It reports a WikiText-2 comparison but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
It does not compare exponents or optimal allocations across fitting choices, setups, or fitting methods.
